My Lord, to seek to maintain a smooth flow of evidence and to combat certain logistical complications as have arisen this morning through traffic difficulties and the like, two matters. One, the evidence will not be presented in necessarily chronological order.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr C] will give her evidence first, and secondly, at three points in time today we will play video representations to ensure that there are no unnecessary gaps.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr Driver.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Jury, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
May I recall [Dr C], please. I state for the record that there is a reporting condition attaching to this witness and her evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [DR C] (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
I appreciate you have been with us previously, but could you state for the record your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I'm [Dr C].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And I'm sure you appreciate you're still bound by the same oath or affirmation that you took previously --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- when you were with us to give evidence pertaining to [Baby E]. And I assume you'll anticipate that you've been invited here today to answer questions relating to his twin brother, [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you a treating physician in relation to [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I didn't have any direct care with him. I was one of the consultants covering a hot week system towards the end of his admission at Chester when some of his blood results came back but I didn't have an active treating role.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll go to those results and consider where they fall on our chronology. With Mr Murphy's assistance, please, could we go to tile 381.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It records that a junior colleague of yours, Dr Katherine Lyddon, F2. Decode that for us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's a foundation level 2 doctor, that's someone in their second year of training after qualifying from university, their second year of practical training.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So with the greatest of respect to the doctor, a very junior colleague of yours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could we click behind and see her notes. Go to the original, please. Scroll down.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Firstly, let's look at -- scroll down to 13 August at 10.30. Would the process be, could you confirm or elaborate, this doctor being such a junior colleague of yours, that her findings on examination or any data received by that doctor would be reported upstream, as it were, to you, her consultant?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. Either directly or indirectly through the other junior doctors in between her level and mine.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. So decoding this note for us, does it read that she, Dr Lyddon, received information from, firstly, the Liverpool Women's Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It would seem pertaining to some genetic tests or checks that had been undertaken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. So [Baby F], as part of his antenatal management, was found to be at high risk of having trisomy 21 or Down's syndrome, so he had genetic tests sent following his birth. He didn't show any clinical features suggestive of that, but those can be difficult to spot in a preterm baby so one of my colleagues had requested the genetic tests. That shows no evidence of trisomy 21 or Down's syndrome. So that's a sort of interim result that means that Down's syndrome is extremely unlikely.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So data recorded antenatally caused the test to be undertaken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And is that routine when those antenatal indicators reach a certain threshold?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But the results, as reported, from the testing hospital, as it were, Liverpool Women's Hospital, who undertook such tests on behalf of the Countess, came back negative --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- in short? The next set of data or information reads:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Hypo screen results."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you decode that for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. A hypo screen stands for hypoglycaemia screen, which is a set of blood tests we do when a baby has profound or persistent low blood sugars to try and see whether there's an underlying cause for that. Some of those tests are performed at the Countess and some of them are sent to another lab in Liverpool, so it sometimes takes some time to get those results back.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, is it right that this sort of test would and was sent to the Royal Liverpool Hospital as opposed to the Liverpool Women's Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, that's my understanding.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you able to interpret the results that were returned and received by -- considered by Dr Lyddon on 13 August?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. The cortisol is a stress hormone in the body and that's a normal level.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The insulin level is -- insulin is a hormone that is made by the body in the pancreas to help regulate blood sugar. It's also a medicine that can be given as a drug. This insulin level is too high for a baby who has a low blood sugar. If a baby has a low blood sugar, you would expect their body to stop making insulin and for the insulin level to be low.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll return to that in a moment. Let's work our way down the remaining data.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: When insulin is made in the body, it's made with Cpeptides stuck to the insulin molecule. Then when the insulin is released, the C-peptide breaks off from the body's own insulin.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you enlighten us as to the relationship, one would anticipate between insulin and C-peptide levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: If insulin was insulin that had been made by [Baby F]'s body, I would expect there to be a similar ratio of insulin to C-peptide, so I would expect the insulin C-peptide to also be high as well. And the fact that this is low means that it's likely that it was insulin given as a drug or as a medicine rather than insulin from [Baby F]'s own body.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As to that likelihood, we'll hear from, with great respect, from experts --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, I would appreciate that, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- in due course.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Someone with greater expertise than you in relation to this.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We did hear something of this from Dr Beech very briefly, but you're giving more details here in relation to this result.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But to recap, in short, naturally generated or created insulin, the levels of such insulin should be reflected --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: -- by the levels of C-peptide?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. It's not an exact match, but you'd expect that to be raised significantly as well.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the two are directly proportionate to each other?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And hence these readings, what would they inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: They strongly suggest to me that [Baby F] has been given insulin as a medicine, which -- the fact that the insulin is high is physiologically inappropriate and the fact that the Cpeptide is low suggests that's insulin given as a medicine. This is something that we found very confusing at the time because [Baby F] had only been prescribed insulin 5 days previously.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We also looked to see if any other babies on the neonatal unit had been prescribed insulin at that time period, thinking about an accidental administration issue, and couldn't -- there weren't any other babies being given insulin at that time, so we were at a bit of a loss as to how to explain this.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's break that up into parts, if I may. You said the insulin level, ie the 4657 reading, was physiologically inappropriate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you explain that in (overspeaking) terms for us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Your insulin levels should fluctuate based on what your blood sugar is doing, so if you have a low blood sugar, your body should stop making insulin. There are some medical conditions where that doesn't happen, but the C-peptide being low makes those more unlikely.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the Countess, you, and we know from tests undertaken by nurses that this baby presented with low blood sugar levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that the basis upon which you deem that reading, 4657, to be physiologically inappropriate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that conclusion 1?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Conclusion 2: given that the insulin levels were recorded at 4657, the C-peptide levels did not correspond to that which you would expect if this was naturally generated insulin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, correct.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because that should be high too?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. My normal response for investigations that don't fit with what I would expect to see would be to repeat them to confirm that that definitely is the case. But because insulin fluctuates, depending on what your blood sugar is doing, because by this period of time [Baby F]'s blood sugars were now stable and normal there was no way to repeat those results.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To return to something else you told us, you queried whether or not he, [Baby F], had received manufactured insulin —
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- man-made insulin --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- as a medicine?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And you said in evidence that he had received some but, your words, 5 days before this, 13 August?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. No, 5 days before his period of profound hypoglycaemia. I think it was in the early hours of 31 July, although that can be checked on the prescriptions, that he received some intravenous insulin with the trade name Actrapid. It's very much -- as it says on the tin, that's a rapid-acting form of insulin and most of the effect of that stops within 15
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: minutes of that no longer infusing. So several days later I would expect all of the effect of that insulin to have long gone from [Baby F]'s body.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is it a matter of record that [Baby F] received that Actrapid very soon after birth, in the first day or so of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The first few days, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that unusual in a preterm baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No. Some preterm babies do have problems maintaining their blood sugar and will have a high blood sugar, which requires treatment with insulin.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So let's return to Dr Lyddon's note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "D/W [discussed with] [you]"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then in note form, that which you've given to us in evidence:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Insulin high, C-peptide low. Unusual for hypoglycaemia [low blood sugar]."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the next comment?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "As now well and sugars stable for no further investigations."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That alludes to the point I mentioned earlier that unusual or unexpected blood results I would always ideally like to repeat, just to confirm what we're dealing with, but that wasn't possible because of his blood sugars now being stable.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the low blood sugar issue had by now, ie by the time of the receipt of this data from the Royal Liverpool Hospital to the Countess on 13 August, they'd resolved?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the final entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "If hypoglycaemia again at any point for repeat screen."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's basically saying if [Baby F] was to have any further episodes of low blood sugar then at that point we should aim to repeat those investigations.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So as a marker for the future. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was anything done with this data or was it acted upon in any way at that time other than that marker?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I think we... I recall looking to see whether anyone else had been given insulin to see whether there was any possibility of an accidental administration but nothing else was done at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And that, that investigation, that review, was that undertaken throughout the neonatal unit or just the particular nursery that [Baby F] was in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No, throughout the whole neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the question was: was anybody prescribed insulin at the time --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- that [Baby F] was presenting with low blood sugar levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Answer no; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you remain there and answer any further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS

Just this, [Dr C]: one of the reasons that there was no further action than that was that in fact, once we get past 5 August, [Baby F]'s blood sugar seemed to be stable and there wasn't a repeat of whatever it was that had caused the issue?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, that's my understanding.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it was just that at that time that there were no babies on the unit who were prescribed insulin. Can you just identify the time more specifically?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: That period of 4 to 5 August where [Baby F] had his low blood sugars.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. So the 4th and the 5th?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, the 4th and the 5th.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for coming back and giving evidence. I don't know, are you coming back again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Not that I'm currently aware.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. In which case thank you for coming on the occasions that you have and giving evidence to this court. Please do not communicate in any way with anyone else about this case until it's all over or anything to do with this case. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)

My Lord, the next witness to call has been delayed but is expected relatively soon. However, rather than invite the court to break at this point, may we play for the jury a video demonstrating the use of some equipment that is relevant to this part of the case and the considerations pertaining to [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: RC.16.21, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)
We seem to have come to an abrupt end there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I will review that in due course. I wasn't expecting it to finish at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It didn't sound as though it had reached a finishing point at all.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We were expecting another 90 seconds. It can only be that the transfer of this video to Mr Murphy's system has been flawed in some way because the version we've looked at previously is a little longer.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Ninety seconds longer?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ninety seconds longer. May we come back to that later today?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll come back. There was a lot of information in that particular video, but it's helpful to see the practical side of it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Later today we'll be calling one of the nurses who involved herself in this sort of application with [Baby F] and we can replay it with that witness and she can assist us as to any detail.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Just in case, I don't know, there was a lot of information there and I expect the jury will want to see that, either in its entirety or parts of it again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll replay it with [Nurse C] later today.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: May I recall Dr John Gibbs, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could I invite you to state your name for the record, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs, as I'm sure you appreciate, you are still bound by the oath or affirmation that you took when you were last with us. We've invited you here this morning to provide evidence in relation to [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you just remind the jury as to your professional status as of August 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was a consultant paediatrician working at the Countess of Chester Hospital at that time and I was the consultant of the week when [Baby F] and his twin brother were born.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you remind the jury what came with being consultant of the week?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It meant that all the babies born that week came under the care of myself or whoever else would have been consultant of the week. In Chester at that time, we covered the paediatric ward as well as the neonatal unit. The consultant would do a ward round, a full ward round, of the babies on the neonatal unit on a Wednesday and a Sunday, but also visited the unit every other day to check on how the babies were doing but didn't examine them all unless there was a particular issue.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: One point that I didn't make last time I gave evidence that I think is quite important is that that style of covering a neonatal unit as well as a paediatric ward is common for a district general hospital. It is the practice that we'd followed for many years prior to 2015 and we weren't complacent about whether we were offering appropriate care for babies on the unit. We carefully monitored activity on the unit and each year we would look at the outcome measures, and a particular one, a crude but important one, was the number of babies who died on the unit. And every year up to 2015, our number of deaths on the neonatal unit were within the range expected for a unit of our type within our region, less than the national average, and yet with that same style of consultant cover, in 2015/2016, the number of deaths increased significantly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it wasn't the style of having to cover the neonatal unit and the paediatric ward that accounted for the change in deaths in 2015.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Gibbs. A professional elsewhere has the responsibility of noting the evidence given by witnesses and I've just received some feedback to the effect that the evidence you have just given was delivered too quickly for that person to keep up with the note. That explains why my attention was being drawn from behind.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the system that you've just described, the consultant of the week with overall clinical responsibility for all the patients —
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, assisted by our junior doctors and nurses.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: By a hierarchy of junior doctors and nurses was, is this right -- if I seek to summarise that which you have just said to us, had been in place for -- how many years did you say?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Oh, many years. I can't -- I think the whole 20 years I'd been in Chester.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it was in place for those 20 years which began?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: 1994 for me in Chester.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. And when did you cease to be a practising consultant at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did the same system prevail throughout?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, it had changed later on, so that we had a consultant of the week on the neonatal side and a consultant of the week on the paediatric ward, but that changed after 2016.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Different consultants, obviously -- or was --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Some additional consultants were appointed, but they were the same consultants who were working there, plus a couple of additional consultants.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It is me being pedantic here: but the same person would not fulfil the role of consultant of the week in the neonatal unit and the paediatric ward?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's what I thought you meant but I just wanted --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Those sort of changes have happened in many district general hospitals in the last few years.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is the evidence you were giving that whilst the same structures were in place for decades, from one particular year there was a marked difference in outcomes?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. A marked difference in the number of deaths and the unusual and unexpected nature of those deaths.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll return to that with you in due course, but could I ask you for the moment, again, please to focus your attention on late July and early August of 2015 when you'd confirmed for us that you were consultant of the week when [Baby F] and his twin brother [Baby E] were born, which was on 29 July 2015.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So does it follow that during that week, you would have, from time to time, concerned yourself with the
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: details of [Baby F]'s welfare, development and any clinical events that may have occurred in that time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And during that time I saw him myself and examined him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Have you been provided with and taken the opportunity of reminding yourself of the details of the clinical notes pertaining to [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Could we take Dr Gibbs, please, to our tile number 5, which records measurements taken on 29 July, which was, as you've already confirmed, his first day of life, to the effect that, in summary, your junior colleague Dr Sally Ogden recorded on the clinical notes, amongst other things, that [Baby F] was presenting with a glucose level of 1.9. We can actually look at Dr Ogden's note, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: These are notes pertaining to [Baby F] shortly after his birth; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In terms of blood glucose levels, what was noted and recorded and interpreted from that data at this point in time? If we keep going up, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His very first glucose level you can see at the bottom of the page disappearing, it says "sugar 2.7", so that's satisfactory, we like it above 2.6 for a premature baby, but that was soon after birth.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall what happened soon thereafter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The next -- it says "repeat gas" there on the page. And the glucose now is 1.9, so it has dropped, which is not uncommon in small babies, premature babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: After delivery they are cut off from the supply from their mum, the nutrition from their mum and sometimes the blood sugar can fall in the first few hours of life.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that's just a natural consequence of the separation of baby from mother?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and more likely to happen the more premature and the smaller a baby is.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And what, if any, response is typically or was provided in relation to [Baby F] for those clinical -- that clinical presentation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, at this time [Baby F] was struggling with his breathing, so he needed some support, and he needed some fluids, so he was started on an infusion of fluids that contained glucose.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we go back to the carousel, please, to tile number 9.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Click on there, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you familiar with documents of this nature, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it's recording the blood gases taken from [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there anything else you want to observe from this document and the data contained on it? What do you note in relation to his blood sugar levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause). I can't see the blood sugar levels on there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I can see the second to last column is headed "lactate".
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not sure the blood sugar levels are on there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: They're appearing now.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right we can see it's written "glucose 15.1". So that's a blood sugar level. That's on his second day of life -- he was born on 29th, that's on the 30th July -- and that's a high level. We roughly aim to keep the babies above 2.6 glucose levels but it shouldn't go often above 7. That's a high level of 15.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What, if any, interpretation would you make as to the changes between those two readings that we've looked at?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, obviously the glucose level has risen to an abnormally high amount. That can happen just because a baby is premature and small and they don't always produce enough insulin themselves to keep the blood sugar at a normal level so the blood sugar can run high.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Sometimes a high blood sugar is an indication of infection and I think at this time [Baby F] had already been started on antibiotics for possible infection.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And a single high blood sugar level -- we would normally just monitor that. A low blood sugar level is more hazardous for a baby. A high blood sugar level leads to complications in the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: longer term and we would monitor that, but it remained high the next one at 00.22 on the 31st, where it is shown as 13.9. So because it remained high, he was started on an insulin infusion at that stage on the second day of life.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So at 21.57 on 30 July, a reading of 15.1.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: High, you tell us. At 00.22 into 31 July, 13.9, obviously lower than the previous reading but still high?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And so was it that second reading that caused the introduction of insulin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't be sure exactly when the insulin started. We'd need to look at the insulin infusion chart, but because the blood sugar remained high that would be an indication for starting insulin. In very small dose, very carefully controlled.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. What effect does stress or infection have on small premature infants' capacity to absorb glucose into the bloodstream?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It reduces the capacity to absorb it from the bloodstream into the body tissues, and therefore stress or infection can cause a high blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Go to tile number 10, please. We see the information indicates that medication in the form of Actrapid was started at 03.40 on 31 July. Is that what you have described as the start of a lowdose insulin infusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's right. In fact, looking at that timing, the junior doctors at the time waited until there were a couple of high blood sugar levels before starting that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go to tile 11, please. We can see that about an hour after the start of that Actrapid infusion, the insulin infusion, a subsequent blood gas chart/blood glucose level reading indicated a level of 8.7.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So what would you have interpreted from that development?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That [Baby F] had responded well to the low-dose insulin infusion and his blood sugar was reducing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As to an individual's capacity to respond or predisposition to respond to insulin infusion, does it vary from individual to individual, from baby to baby, or is it fairly predictable?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's reasonably predictable, which is why we give insulin in very low dose and monitor the blood sugars carefully. Because you would expect a fairly prompt reduction in blood sugar once you start insulin.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that is what happened here?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did the baby's blood glucose level continue to fall in response to the introduction of this infusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it remained lower, which is why the insulin infusion was stopped after just a few hours.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go to the next tile, which records the time at which it was ceased, and so, no pun intended, did the Actrapid have a rapid response?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and it was stopped after about 3 hours.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that what's intended, is that what it's for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Sometimes insulin may need to continue for a little longer but [Baby F] responded very well and did not require the insulin after that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could move on through the carousel, please, just slide across and see... Let's move on, please, and could we put up Dr Gibbs' first introduction here.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right.

blocks.text: Your handwriting, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is.

blocks.text: Could I ask you to pause there. I anticipate the notetaker might be struggling again. This reference here with the arrow pointing upwards?

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Initially, [Baby F] was started on full intravenous fluids, but then gradually some nasogastric milk feeds had been introduced and in that entry there, saying "fluids", just beneath "drugs", I have pointed out that he's on TPN, that's the intravenous nutrition, but he was also receiving 5ml every 2 hours and EBM, which is expressed breast milk, so his mother's milk, through a nasogastric tube, so he was receiving some intravenous feeding, some nasogastric milk feeds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We have heard, and could you confirm, that as for TPN, babies receiving TPN would receive a Start-up pack -- a bag, I should say, not pack?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which is standardised in content?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Then a more mature mix of nutrition after that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, we still tended to use standard bags, but we could then add in extra salts if we needed to by separate infusion.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As the need required?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As required, yes. But [Baby F] at this stage was managing on just the ordinary standard TPN.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. The next set of notes (overspeaking) subheading "on examination" --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, on examination, [Baby F] was in air, so he wasn't requiring any additional oxygen. But he'd had that morning some intermittent desats, that's desaturations, temporary drops in his blood oxygen level. But he was on CPAP, the form of respiratory support at the time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I should add he was gradually improving from full ventilation to BiPAP to CPAP, so he was moving in an encouraging direction with decreased support needed for his breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If within that positive evolution there were intermittent desaturations, would that have been a cause of concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not by themselves, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It says "mild subcostal recession". That just means he was sucking in his tummy a little bit below his ribs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That is an indication of increased work of breathing and very common in premature babies. And "clear breath sounds" means his lungs sounded clear when I listened with a stethoscope.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the heart sounds, the first and second heart sounds, plus nil else heard, and that's why I've recorded I couldn't hear his heart murmur but I did add that the CPAP machine makes quite a loud noise and I didn't want to turn it off to examine him, so I couldn't hear a murmur above the CPAP noise.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So drowned out by background noise?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, or indeed there may have been no murmur there at all.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then it says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Soft flat abdomen. Active on handling."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All encouraging signs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, could you scroll down to J2928, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I then come to my impression of how [Baby F] was doing at the end. As noted, although he was in air on CPAP, intermittently he had desaturations, drops in his oxygen. The nurses had tried him off the CPAP support that morning before I examined him and his oxygen saturation dropped. That's what I'm noting there, he did need some increased oxygen intermittently but I felt it was likely the result of respiratory distress syndrome, the RDS, from which he was recovering, but I felt we ought to check or recheck his C-reactive protein, the CRP, which
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: is an indication of infection because he was going to have other blood tests done that day, that's why I say:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Recheck the CRP with his urea and electrolytes and [bilirubin]."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Bili" is bilirubin.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. And finally for this examination of the baby that morning on your ward round?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because [Baby F] was doing well, the plan was to increase his nasogastric milk as tolerated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm grateful to Mr Murphy, who reminds me that I ought to inform everybody that these two pages of the clinical notes are available in the additional file on everybody's iPad.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And it's 2597 and 2598?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's for our reference, Dr Gibbs. I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So taking up where your note left off, moving forward to his 7th day of life and 5 August, were his milk feeds steadily increased as per the plan here?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we look, please, behind tile 161, we see reference to Dr Harkness. If we can scroll down for Dr Harkness' entry. At 01.30 on 5 August 2015, "R/V", is that...? "R/V"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Review.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Review. Do you know whether this was a routine review or in response to the events that are recorded?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe it was in response to a concern about the vomiting and the increased heart rate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll hear from Dr Harkness in due course, but would the need for this review have been overseen by you as the consultant of the week?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was ultimately responsible, but at the time, at 1.30 in the morning, Dr Harkness was on the night shift and I was on call at home.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Was this brought to your attention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Later on, at about 3.30 in the morning, Dr Harkness phoned me.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So let's consider what it was that Dr Harkness reviewed at the time at 1.30. Did you in due course -were you in due course told that there were multiple small milky vomits and 9ml of milky aspirate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The baby's heart rate was at 200 beats per minute?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, which was quite high, even for a premature baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The other observations recorded there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, really, Dr Harkness finds otherwise a well-looking [Baby F] really from what he's observed. He's saying the abdomen is not distended -- that is a little diagram on the left-hand side. Chest is clear, he's put on the right-hand side. He does hear a heart murmur. So the baby looked well but had been vomiting and had an unusually fast heart rate. In fact, the observation chart from this time at night shows a sudden increase up to over 200, which is very unusual.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that's the nurses or the observation chart completed by the nurses monitoring on an hourly basis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it's suddenly increased from a normal rate up to over 200.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What, if any, interpretation was made of those factors, whether together or in isolation, the multiple small, milky vomits, the milky aspirate, and the sudden elevation of heart rate that you just alluded to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At this time, from talking to me on the phone, Dr Harkness had assumed it could be due to infection and I agreed with that, but it's still unusual to have such a sudden change in observations. The reason the nurses undertake observations is to give us warning when patients are deteriorating, but little [Baby F] had suddenly gone from being stable to having a very fast heart rate, plus some vomiting. So it was a very rapid change, even for infection.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But infection, if not treated, can be very serious which is why Dr Harkness had, as you'll see in a moment, gone on to treat [Baby F] as if he may have an infection, and when he spoke to me a little later by phone I felt that was appropriate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could we scroll down, please. We see something signed by Dr Wood there. Are we able to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Wood is the SHO, a more junior junior doctor working with Dr Harkness. It says the plan is to re-screen, that's to recheck for infection, and start second line antibiotics. They are called second line because [Baby F] was already on antibiotics, he was just about to finish the course he'd started at birth but because he may have had another infection at this stage he was started on different antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the use of the word line here is a reference to the type of antibiotics rather than --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- the route by which (overspeaking) provided?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You could call it second stage antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could we go to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then the "cef" and "teic" is an abbreviation for the cefotaxime and teicoplanin, the two antibiotics that were then started.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can we go to tile 165, please. If we look at the fluids at the right side of the chart, please. I'm inviting Dr Gibbs' attention to the early hours of 5 August and the provision of TPN to [Baby F]. Could we have the dates at the top?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was [Baby F]'s provision of TPN amended in response to the observations recorded by Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The main change at this stage was, because of the vomiting and the fact that when the nurses sucked out the nasogastric tube there was some milk still left in [Baby F]'s stomach after each feed, his nasogastric feeds, milk feeds, were stopped which meant the amount of TPN, the intravenous feeding, needed to be increased.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Previously we had seen a regime of ever-increasing feeds.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Milk feeds through the nasogastric tube, yes. And they were stopped.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: They were stopped and replaced by intravenous TPN, effectively?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, an increased amount of intravenous TPN.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Quite right, which would have been provided to [Baby F] through which method?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe he had a long line at this stage. He needed an intravenous line and he had a long line in his right groin at this stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could then go to tile 163 and J3255, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, just pause for a moment, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: They're having difficulty hearing you, the stenographer.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think it is there. You have to keep your voice up.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I shall.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That's better. Thank you.

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs has got a very good strong voice.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, we can see it's abnormally low at 0.8mmols/litre.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we can see in the column above that how his blood sugar levels had been entirely satisfactory, varying between 3.8 and 6.7 in the previous couple of days.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the 3.8 reading that you've just alluded to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The 0.8, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Second from the bottom.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Previously, if we just take below the hole punch, 3 August 2015, at 09.45 -- that's the one, thank you, Mr Murphy -- 5.4. That's the morning reading.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Late afternoon reading, below it, 15.54 hours, 3.9.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Night-time reading, 21.48 hours, at 5. 4 August, in the morning, at 08.16 hours, 3.8. Then 23.32 hours, on 4 August, 5.5. Then the reading that you've focused upon, 01.54 hours, 0.8.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So that's the first abnormally low reading there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's a worryingly low reading for a baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So what, if any, action was taken upon discovery of that reading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: A bolus of glucose, that's sugar, was given intravenously. And I think around this time, Dr Harkness started an extra infusion with some glucose and salt in addition to the TPN to try and keep the blood sugar up.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we go to tile 172, please, which records at 02.15 hours, in the early hours of Wednesday, 5 August 2015, "pathology blood ordered". If we go behind the tile.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you explain this to us, please, Dr Gibbs? It contains your name.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. This is a result merely showing [Baby F]'s blood group.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's not really relevant to the blood sugar. So he's group A positive.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Let's go back to the carousel then, please, and go to tile 181. Return to the document below. Let's plot his course.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We looked at the penultimate entry, the 0.8 blood sugar reading. You told us of the response to that reading and then we see at 02.55, it had risen to 2.3.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Which is an improvement, which is moderately encouraging but still relatively low because we aim to keep premature babies' blood sugars above 2.6. But it's still an improvement, much improved from 0.8, so the response to this would probably continue to monitor the blood sugar carefully.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the baby was continuing on TPN --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- with 10% dextrose? I think if we go to tile 183, we can see the medications, saline -- if we click behind that and look at the fluids to the right. Magnify the right side of the page, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see a 10% dextrose column.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it's the third column across.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Does that read "commenced"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's about 04 in the morning, it looks like.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And so was that an additional provision in order to maintain higher blood glucose levels in [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: A further blood glucose level was checked at 5 am?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and it's 2.9 in the column.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you. Then if we go, please, behind tile 187, we'll see another entry from Dr Harkness, which includes "Discussed with Dr Gibbs".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we look at that which was recorded by Dr Harkness at 03.30 on 5 August, could you assist us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. [Baby F] had already raised concerns because of his initial vomiting and his fast heart rate and his low blood sugar. At 03.30, Dr Harkness had been reviewing him and because of the fast heart rate, had arranged a ECG, that is electrical recording of the heart. It's probably, but Dr Harkness can answer this, not only because the heart rate was fast because it had so suddenly increased that he wondered whether [Baby F] could have a problem with an abnormal heart rate, an inherent problem with the pacemaker of the heart causing a very fast rhythm. That's called an SVT.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's why, when he's written "Discussed with [D/W] Dr Gibbs", I have said to him it's unlikely to be an SVT, this is an abnormal heart rhythm, simply because usually in a premature baby the heart rate in an SVT would be around 300. And although [Baby F]'s heart rate was abnormally fast at a little over 200, it wasn't fast enough, I felt, to be one of these inherent inborn heart rhythm problems called an SVT.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So then Dr Harkness has written -- he is writing what I have said with him, discussed with them on the phone call:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Suggest repeating fluid bolus."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This is because we had assumed at this stage the fast heart rate, the vomiting, the low blood sugar may be due to infection, and as well as treating the low blood sugar, a fast heart rate could be the result of decreased perfusion, a drop in general perfusion that happens with infection and that's treated by just giving extra fluids.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So some of the boluses of fluid were glucose to get the blood sugar up, some of the boluses of fluid given during the night to [Baby F] at this stage was saline to improve his general circulation in case that was the cause of his abnormally fast heart rate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So at that stage you were considering three features of his presentation: the increased heart rate, the level of the heart rate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The speed at which it had elevated to that level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Unusual for an infection, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And the low blood sugar levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And at that point, at 03.30 hours on the morning of 5 August, what potential causes were under consideration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That [Baby F] may have developed an infection. But that was still unusual to have such a sudden change in his observations.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That he may be dehydrated, but both those, infection and dehydration, were treated by giving him extra fluids. And as discussed, the junior doctors, appropriately at that stage, had started different antibiotics to cover an infection. So we were treating him for infection and a degree of dehydration.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The jury heard earlier this morning from [Dr C], who reported about a blood analysis ultimately received from the Royal Liverpool Hospital to the Countess of Chester on 13 August. And you're appraised of those results, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Knowing of them now, how would you interpret those three features that you've just discussed or given evidence about as per [Baby F]'s presentation at 03.30 on 5 August?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Although there are many causes for fast heart rate and a low blood sugar, the fact that [Baby F] later this day, on 5 August, was found to have an abnormally high level of insulin, in fact an extremely high level of insulin in his blood, in retrospect that now makes it likely that his symptoms he was displaying after midnight on 5 August were related to very low blood sugar, caused by him receiving a high dose of insulin.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That would cause a fast heart rate, that would cause his low blood sugar, and that might also cause him to vomit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could we --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But I didn't suspect that at the time at 3.30 in the morning because there was no reason why he should have had a high dose of insulin administered to him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could we go to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, just before you do, just looking at the note that's still up on the screen of Dr Harkness, "Continue to monitor", and then, "Only for [a word beginning with A] if heart rate around 300".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Could you just tell us that so it doesn't remain a mystery?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Harkness has written:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Only for adenosine..."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which is a drug given to treat the SVT, abnormally fast heart rates, if it's due to an inherent and in-built pacemaker problem with the heart. But I had discussed, I did not think it was an SVT and we shouldn't be considering treating the SVT with this drug, adenosine, unless the heart rate reached 300, which would make it a bit more likely to be an SVT, rather than a response to some form of stress.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. I thought that might be the case but I just wanted your confirmation of it.

blocks.text: Then there's "query query", meaning much less likely, could it be NEC, the necrotising enterocolitis, but I didn't think he had any clinical signs, apart from a fast heart rate and query sepsis, any other clinical signs, particularly on examining his abdomen, to indicate he is likely to have NEC.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Next entry?

blocks.text: Well, they were sent to our biochemistry department in Chester; I am not sure where they sent them to. blocks.text: Well, the first chemical mentioned is cortisol, a stress hormone, and that's measured because sometimes if that is very deficient, you're lacking in cortisol, you can have a low blood sugar, but that blood level is satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But the more relevant result, the next chemical mentioned is insulin. Now, given that this blood test was taken at the time [Baby F]'s blood sugar was abnormally low at 1.3, there should be virtually no insulin detectable in the body -- natural insulin detectable in the body at that stage because of the low blood sugar. And yet rather than being an undetectable level of insulin, it's a very high level of 4,657 picomoles per litre. That's a very high insulin level.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The next chemical mentioned is insulin C-peptide -- has this been discussed in court?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: [Dr C] touched upon it briefly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because when insulin is produced naturally in the body, the insulin molecules attach to this C-peptide and they are broken apart and both are secreted from the pancreas into the blood. The C-peptide stays in the blood much longer than insulin; insulin is removed from the blood within a few minutes. So normally the C-peptide level of natural insulin is much higher in the blood than insulin level. So we've got an insulin level of 4,600-odd. If -- the C-peptide for natural insulin should have been way above 4,600, instead it's undetectable. It says less than 169, but you can see on the right-hand side the normal range for the C-peptide is 190 to 990. The fact the lab said less than 169, it doesn't mean it's 169, it could be zero. It's just very -- it's undetectable by that laboratory's analysis.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So a very low level of C-peptide.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The bottom chemical is a C-peptide/insulin and that's a ratio between C-peptide and insulin. And it says the result there is zero but it give you the normal rain of 5 to 10 and what that means is the C-peptide level in the blood for natural insulin should be 5 to 10 times higher than the insulin level, which means if this had been natural insulin and [Baby F]'s level was 4,600, the C-peptide should have been 5 to 10 times higher so around 20,000 to 40,000. But instead it's undetectable.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So this isn't natural insulin, this is synthetic insulin made by a drug company because it doesn't have any C-peptide attached to it. So it's a very abnormal result to have a high insulin level when there's a low blood sugar. And there are rare disorders that premature babies can suffer from where they secrete, produce, too much insulin themselves. This wasn't one of them, because there should have been a very high C-peptide level and there wasn't. So this insulin result shows that [Baby F] had been given a drug form, a pharmaceutical form, a synthetic form of insulin. But he was never prescribed this at this time and he should never have received it.
